When it wants more than it is wearing it reaches down and takes it, because up there the ground is the same material as the thing standing on it, and there has never once been a shortage.

The chips that come off it are near-black glass with a cold blue sheen, which is an odd thing to be picking up at that height. It is the stuff of the black ground far below that has no business being warm and is. People who have stood on both say the only difference is what got to the rock first, and then talk about something else. The same seam accounts for the eyes, which unsettle people rather more than the size does: a dull red spark down in one socket, no fellow to it in the other, holding steady from every angle you can take. Get a proper look at a broken one and the unsettling stops. The red is a thread in the rock and not a light behind it, and the sockets have no back to them — two holes in a face-shaped stone, about as deep as a thumb, and then solid.

The hard piece in it is not ice either. Grey plated rock with a single bright cyan seam driven through it, pocket-sized and thoroughly unpleasant to keep in a pocket: the whole creature in small, the two materials and the joint between them. What it lends is both at once. Worked into an edge it puts the cold in ahead of the metal, and whatever took the blow spends a while afterwards moving as though the ground had gone knee-deep.

It will still be standing up there when the low country it has never once visited has gone soft twice over. There is nothing in it that could be pleased about that. It has no round to walk, and nothing it is late for, and no name it keeps failing to produce; it goes where the ice is, and comes back, and has been doing that since before the first fires were lit. People who work the high ground say they do not find it frightening. They find it restful, which is its own sort of warning, and after a season of it they come down.

ice_poring.description: Packed snow with two dark eyes, heavier than snow should be. Every spike it throws is grown out of itself.
lore: Low in this country the ground does not stay put. A path takes itself somewhere else between one season and the next; a hill everybody was certain of turns out not to be there, and there is no saying when it stopped. High under the crystal country none of that happens. The snow up there has not needed correcting in a very long time, and there is also hardly anyone left up there to walk on it. What comes up out of that combination is packed harder than anything down in the grass.

It is snow pressed into a shape with two dark eyes set well into it, and it weighs more than snow has any business weighing. What it is packed from does not melt: a handful of the blue-white pebbles that come off one will sit in a warm palm all afternoon and be exactly as cold when it is put down. The parts keep. The whole one does not.

It arms itself out of itself. A spike comes up through the top, grows to a point, and goes — and there is measurably less creature afterwards than there was before it started. It will do that until there is not enough left to do it with, because there is nothing up there to show it another way and nothing in it that could be shown. At the end it does not shatter, which is what people expect and would be easier to watch. It slumps. The shape gives up its edges and goes down into a lump of slush inside its own footprint, and the wet mark outlasts the rest of it by an hour.

In the slush lies a pale blue stone rimed white, cold to hold and staying cold, and warm underneath that in the way they all are. In a blade it puts winter into the hit, and every so often — not reliably, and never on the swing you were counting on — whatever took the hit goes heavy-footed for a while, as though it had walked further uphill than it meant to and only just noticed. That is the high ground pressed down to the size of a fist: the part of the world that has not gone anywhere, standing about in the drifts in quantity, on a road that has stopped having anyone on it.

lava_poring.description: Under a crust of cooled rock, a fistful of heat going out. To strike, it splits along the seams and flares.
lore: There is a stretch of the mountain that is the wrong colour and warm through the boot. No account of why has ever satisfied anybody, and the disagreement is half of what keeps the place going: argued over, walked around, described in detail to people who have never been within a day of it, and hardly ever crossed. Things get up out of ground held that way.

This one is mostly crust. Everybody who ever sat close to a fire remembers the same thing about one, and it is not the flame — it is the black skin that forms over a log late in the evening with the red still moving underneath. Everyone has that part exactly, so that is the part that stood up: a fistful of banked heat in a shell of cooled rock, going out from the moment it got up.

It fights by splitting. The shell opens along its seams, the heat comes out all at once and very bright, and then the shell shuts and there is a little less inside than there was. It cannot do that many times. Nothing about the arrangement suggests it was built to last, and nothing about it suggests it minds.

Coming apart, the light goes first. The yellow drains back out of the seams, the red follows it, and the shell crumbles smaller and smaller until there is not enough left of it to crumble. What is on the ground afterwards is the litter a fire leaves: a faceted lump of orange stone still lit along its splits, a piece or two of black glass keen enough to shave with, and one ember down in the middle of it that will not go out however long you wait.

The ember is the hard piece — scorched dark red, more embers sulking in its cracks, warm in the pocket and warm a hundred years from now. It does not burn hot in a blade. It warms one, and it warms whoever is carrying it, and it takes the worst out of a fire that would otherwise have had the skin off them. Which is right, because what it is the last of was never the burning. It is being warm.

lava_salamander.description: Basks all day, crusted and cracked open on the light beneath, then gets up breathing fire it never learned.
lore: What fell was small. A damp thing the length of a hand, the colour of wet bark and living under it, no danger to anything and in no danger either. That is the animal, entire. There is nothing whatever in it to account for what is out on the black rock now.

Then it thinned, the way everything here thins, and by the time its own account of itself had gone there was a great deal of everybody else's lying about to take up the slack. A great many of the dead handled a creature like this once, in a great many countries, and nearly all of them handled it the same way: you put a log on the fire, and a little while later something comes running out of the flame. Every one of them drew the obvious conclusion. Not one of them ever went back and checked. So the shape it holds now is theirs, and it stands several times the size the animal was: the hide gone to crust, the crust split along the seams, something in the gaps that is steady rather than flickering, and eyes the same colour as the gaps. When the mouth opens what comes out is fire. It is the same animal all the way through, for all that. Nothing got up out of the warm ground out there to replace it; it fell, once, and it was smaller than a hand.

The hard piece is a coal. Dark rock, cracked through, live red still moving in the seams, and as warm the year after as the day it came out; set into a blade it sets alight whatever the blade touches, and the burning carries on a while after you have stopped. Which is odd on the face of it, the fire on the animal having been somebody else's idea to begin with. Except that it was told into burning and then it burned, every day, for a very long time, and there is no line anywhere in that where the borrowed thing stops and the creature's own habit starts. Everything else it leaves goes cold. The shed teeth, the broad amber fang split from crown to root where it came down on the wrong kind of bone, the foot cut clean off at the joint with its three cream claws: warm in the hand for an hour or two, and then only leavings.

It does not appear to hunt. There is very little on that stretch worth the trouble, and it spends most of a day flat against the warm stone doing nothing at all, which is precisely what the story about it says it should be doing. Then it gets up and walks a round that nothing accounts for, and bites whatever is standing in it. The black rock runs toward the cave and gets warmer the whole way. It walks to the edge of that and turns, every time, and has never gone in.

lava_salamander_2.description: Dull olive, pale flat eyes, a gape wider than the skull carrying it. One bite. Rarely two.
lore: The Chronicle files this one beside the burning one because at forty paces they have the same silhouette, and there the resemblance stops. Nothing about this animal is on fire. It is the colour of lichen on a north face, dull olive going grey, mottled so finely that if it holds still against wet stone there is nothing there to see. The eyes are the wrong colour for eyes, flat and pale and pinkish at the inner corner, and it fell out of a life spent in water under stone, in the dark, where they cannot have been much use to it either. What it did bring down with it was the jaw. The head is most of the creature and the jaw is most of the head, hinged much further back than looks reasonable, so that the gape comes out wider than the skull carrying it. One bite, delivered without any preamble at all, and generally that is the encounter.

What it does now is take the hard things. Bone first: it will spend an entire night on a single marrow bone and leave it knobbed, stained and lying in the open, which is how anyone knows one is working an area. Bone is only where it starts. Stone gets chewed; what cannot be chewed gets swallowed; and of everything on that mountain that will not soften or wear or go anywhere, the best by a long way is gold, which it takes whenever it finds any, though not one of these creatures has ever been opened up with gold still inside it. There is no mystery in the appetite once you have watched this country for a season. Everything else goes. A hillside goes, a path goes, a fat reliable thing you were counting on goes soft where it stands and then is not anywhere at all. A creature that will only take what refuses to go is, in its blunt way, the most sensible thing on that mountain, and it has never at any point known that about itself. It works ground that other things have quietly stopped working, nearer the cave than anything out there that still has an inside.

The paws it sheds are never a matching pair: three pale curled claws on a scrap of mottled hide, and the next one off the same animal is subtly the wrong shape. Whatever grows back after a loss comes back approximate, and the one after that comes back approximate from the approximation. The hard piece prised out of the jaw carries that whole history in a single object, sea-green and broken clean through, the break filled in with gold. The mend gets explained two ways and both ways have people who will swear by them: that the gold is everything hard the creature ever took, gone at last to the one part of it that could hold anything; or that the crack came first and the gold went in after, and the appetite was only ever the animal trying to get back what it had already lost. Worked into armour it makes the armour hold, and carried about it seems to arrange for gold to turn up.

malformed_creature.description: Bare, blotched, hairless and shaped exactly like a person, coming at a walk with one hand open and green.
lore: Out on the black rock, where the ground is warm underfoot, something walks that is exactly the shape of a person. Bare, hairless, not a stitch on it, the head a little large for the body, skin blotched in patches that do not match one another. Nothing about it is monstrous in the way that word usually goes. The masked ones drop a face in the dirt when they go down; this one never took the face off, and wears the whole thing, all over, all the time.

It kept the belongings too, and that is the part people find hard. A bronze locket knotted over with spirals, worn in under the skin. A pitted silver band still sitting on a finger, plainly never made for that hand. Grave dirt worked into the creases. A bundle of long pale bones on a cord, carried. Half a spool of plain linen thread. Every one of those is a fact about somebody with the somebody taken out of it, and the people who go through what one of these leaves behind are not robbing it so much as reading it. No name has ever been read off one.

It follows, and it does not hurry. Upright, arms hanging and never swinging, which is what tells you at fifty paces, because a person's arms swing and this one's do not. When it arrives it does not bite and it does not claw. It reaches. An open hand, out and across, a gesture anybody would recognise, and everyone who has met one says that is the worse thing. What comes off the hand is green. There is green in the seams of it under the blotching, and by every account it is what holds the shape upright now; where the skin has parted it weeps. It does not clear out of a wound. It settles, and the next one settles on top of that, and the next on top of that again. Nothing about this creature ever subtracts.

Why the outside is the part that lasted has a tidy account, and the people fondest of it are the ones who have not been out there. It runs like this: the outside of a person is the part other people hold — a face, a build, the set of a hand doing nothing, kept by every acquaintance who ever passed it in a doorway — while the inside was only ever held by the one occupant. That is a decent account of skin still walking and no account at all of the rest. Not of what did the taking. Not of why it went all at once instead of over an age. Not of why it is happening now, and here, on ground where none of this used to happen. Break one and it puts its hands down first, the way something might that half remembers kneeling, then folds up small, and the colour washes out of it, blotches and flush and all, until there is a pale heap on the warm rock getting flatter. The stone is in there: cobbled grey, green still leaking from every joint of it, warm in the palm, and warm and leaking in a hundred years. Harder to put down is where the heap was. A long way round the massif from any way into the cave that anybody knows, and it was not out there on its own.

mammoth.description: Crowd it and one sweep of ivory clears the road. Otherwise it grazes, wool to the ankles, a herd of one.
lore: Nothing else grazing this country comes anywhere near it for size. Dark brown wool hangs off it nearly to the ankles, the shoulder stands over a grown person, and the tusks come out cream and curve up and out far enough to clear a path on their own. It grazes ground with very little left in it: the molars that come out of one are worn flat past anything grass would account for. What surprises people who expect trouble from something that size is how uninterested it is. Nothing about it is hunting. Nothing about it was ever posted to watch anything. It shifts what is in front of it the way weather shifts things, without attitude, and nearly everything that has ever gone wrong between one of these and a person went wrong because the person stood too close for too long. Crowd it and the head comes round, and one sweep of that ivory ends the conversation.

The spacing is the part to watch. It keeps a gap open on either side of itself. It halts the way an animal halts when the animal ahead of it has halted. It will stand for long stretches in the middle of open ground doing nothing in particular, at the correct interval from nothing in particular. That is herd behaviour, performed accurately, by one animal, and whatever came down out of the sky alongside it is not here to complete the arrangement.

Bringing one down is not like bringing down the small things. The knees go first, and that takes a while. Then it settles into the grass. Then the whole enormous thing goes pale at once, wool and hide and ivory together, while the outline stays exactly where it was — and then the outline goes as well. People who have watched that once do not go out of their way to watch it again, because for a moment it looks like the thing everybody in this country is actually afraid of. It is not that, and the flattened grass is the proof, because there is something lying in it: a piece of ivory small enough to close a hand around, chalk-cream, webbed all over with fine fissures, and warm. The largest thing anybody has met out there comes down to something that fits in a fist, which is either the most even-handed fact in Nangijala or the most unpleasant one, depending on who is holding it. And it could not have been anything else. What this animal knows better than any other is not breaking. The tusks it sheds are snapped clean off at the root by something that never once broke stride, and every fissure in that stone is a break it kept walking after. Set into armour it lends precisely that, which is not strength. It is the habit of continuing while damaged.

masked_shadow_creature.description: Not a thing that thinned — a thing that was emptied. Whatever moved in kept the face, and the mask is all it leaves.
lore: Everything else in the wild is running on habit — a shape that outlasted whoever was inside it, going patiently through the last motions it ever learned. Grinmask is not that, and anyone who has met both can tell within a heartbeat.

It was emptied. Not over centuries, the ordinary way, with the details going gently and nobody at any point in distress. All at once, the way a room is emptied, and something else moved into the space that was left.

What is in there now is a sliver of moving dark, and it is not the creature's own. It is wearing the outside. This is why it does not behave like anything else out there: a thing at the stage of Habit is uninterested in you and will only hurt you because you walked into its round, but Grinmask skips. It plays. It has a preference about being watched. There is somebody's intention operating in that shape and it did not come from the shape.

Break it and the dark simply stops being there — no struggle, no leaving, it is present and then it is not. What falls is the mask, which lands in the dirt and does not thin. It sits there being exactly a face for as long as anybody leaves it, long after everything else about the creature has stopped being anywhere at all.

It is still smiling. It was always going to be smiling. A face is the easiest part of a person to remember and the last part to let go, and the mask is not a disguise the creature put on. It is the only piece of the original that the emptying did not take.

This is the observation that started the whole investigation into the eastern mountain, and the masks are still the best evidence anyone has of what is down there. Nobody has yet explained why a hungry thing should bother leaving the faces behind.

mystical_frog.description: A green weight in the shallows, in no hurry to move, and the first thing a great many new stars ever meet.
lore: Animals fall too. The sky drops them at the same rate it drops people and sorts neither, and where a new star gets met and told what has happened to it, a frog does not, because there is nothing useful anyone can say to a frog. This one came down in the wet and carried on with the only trade it had. Sit where the flies come. Hold still. Be cold. Be patient past the point where patience is a virtue and out the far side of it, where patience is simply what a thing is made of.

That is very nearly all there is to a frog, which is what makes it so hard to say how far down this one has got. When a person loses their particulars it shows. A frog that has lost every one of its own sits in the shallows in exactly the attitude it always sat in. It has not needed to eat for longer than most of the roads have been where they are, and it still waits where the flies would come. Under it in the silt is a smooth grey-blue stone, worn round by more water than it has sat in since, cold in the palm however long the day has been — and every round wet thing out in the ponds keeps one as well.

The low end of the meadows is where people walk when they have just come down and cannot yet say their own name, so this is very often the first thing anybody meets here: a green weight the size of two hands with a hard yellow eye on each side of its head, looking back and not getting up. Going out to meet a star is the oldest courtesy in this world. The frog is not keeping it; the frog was only already there, which for a great many arrivals has had to be near enough. It is also, very often, the first thing anybody breaks — it is close, it is slow, it does not run — and afterwards somebody is standing shin-deep in cold water with a small warm stone in their hand, mottled the green of the water round their shins and already quietly at work on their knuckles. Sitting in the wet and coming out of the sitting in slightly better repair than it went in was the whole of what the animal could do. Most people begin exactly this way. The first kindness this country does them, they take off a thing that was only sitting there.

night_beast.description: Dark hide split at the shoulders and spine, lit bone standing up through it. You see one coming a long way off.
lore: On all fours, hunched, with long arms and hands that end in fingers rather than paws, and quicker on that hunch than a thing built like that has any right to be. The hide is dark and split: along the shoulders, down the whole length of the spine, at the flanks. Standing up through the splits is bone, pale, carrying its own light. The head is bone the whole way round, two sockets in it and nothing you can find in them that is looking back.

Everything else out in that country is at some stage of going. A shape with the details gone but the round still walked. A shape with nothing left in it but the last thing it ever learned. Then, in its own time, nothing. This one is at no stage at all. It did not get here the slow way; it went into the ground one way and came out the other, and where the long accounting ought to be there is a light instead, and the light has not gone down by so much as a shade.

Keepers who worked the eastern circuit used to say there was one mercy left near the mouth and this was it, a thing that cannot cross a black wood without announcing itself. They stopped saying it after somebody watched one hunt. The light is not leaking and it is not for your benefit. It comes up out of the ribs at whatever is standing close in front, and anything that has been in an unlit place long enough to have given up on light goes blind where it stands and is still standing there, blind, when the long raking arm arrives. The crouch, the reach, the arm — all of it is built for coming out of the dark, and the light is the part that does the work.

Bone is all that comes off it, and nothing stranger than bone: ribs bleached clean, hooked talons in matched sets, some of them the same grey hooks the horned fiends shed, a marrow bone knobbed at both ends and stained where beige should not be. It bleeds, too, and freely, which is not what people expect from something that was emptied. Breaking it goes wrong in a particular way. It comes apart at the neck, the lit head leaves first, and the rest of it stays up on its hands a moment afterwards, which is the part that anyone who has seen it gets to in the telling and then skips. The hard piece is dark and banded, with a seam of live gold in it that has not gone out and is not going to, warm, and impossible to forget. It is the same light that was in the bones: in a weapon it burns what it touches, and close in it does to other things exactly what the ribs did. That light was burning in there the whole time it was out in that country. It was never once lit for anybody.

saber_toothed_tiger.description: A hunter left over from an age this country stopped telling, black-furred, amber-eyed, built for one rush.
lore: The fangs are longer than the jaw can shut over, so the mouth has to open the whole way before they are any use at all, and when it does you can see how little of the rest of the animal was built for anything else. Coat like wet coal. Eyes the colour of a lamp turned low. It came down out of a country far enough back that nothing walking around today has seen one of these standing up in life, and it has been out in the grass, more or less unmentioned, ever since.

Unmentioned is most of what is wrong with it. Other things get talked about badly — at the wrong fire, by somebody who only half saw them — and badly is still being held. This one does not come up. So it has gone the way untold things go, and the order is the sad part: the plain went first, then the weather on the plain, then whatever it used to be afraid of, then the others of its kind strung out along the line of a hunt. What is still out in the grass is the last hundred yards of one. It will lie in the open for hours doing nothing whatever, calm the way a cat is calm, which is not calm at all but a decision that has not been taken yet.

The leavings are honest about it. Coarse black mats of coat with other things' quills caught in them, off an animal that tried its luck on something quilled and ought to have walked past. A matched pair of glossy hooks, as sharp as the day they grew. Now and then a tooth hollowed at the root and gilded bright by somebody who thought the occasion called for that, and whoever it was is not around to say what the occasion had been. And under all of it, the piece that will not go any further down: grey, plated, shut around a clot of red. Of everything the animal used to be, what lasted was the part that took something back out of whatever it opened. Held against a blade it goes on doing exactly that, and it does not know how to do it by halves.

None of that came out of a telling. It was got by walking out to where one lies up and watching for a long while. The tellers will point out that being looked at is not the same as being told about; whoever wrote this down did not argue the point, and wrote it down.

snow_demon.description: Gaunt, four-horned, snow to the claws. The wings never beat. Two colours on it are wrong, and both are hot.
lore: The snow it stands in is the same colour it is, crest of the head down to the claws, so the first thing anybody sees of one is the eyes. Lean, hard, hunched forward at the shoulders. Four ivory horns off a single base, ridged like bark. Long hooked claws, grown in sets. Wings held open and never once beaten — it has had them the whole time and it comes at you on its feet. Then the specks: a rust-coloured scatter across the hide, the other wrong colour up there, since nothing that high makes rust. No fire is kept that high, no rota ever ran that far, no round goes up there at all, so there is no account of what this was to hold the thing walking around now up against. The ones found lower down can at least be argued about.

Everything on it is the colour and the temperature of the mountain, and the stone inside it is neither. Black, pebbled, a cyan vein running through it, and the vein moves. Worked into a blade it throws a spark that now and then does not stop where it lands: it carries on, from the body it found to the next body along. That mismatch is the argument about this one, and the argument is live. The people who work the high snow find no mystery in it and say so patiently — dry cold is the country that bites you when you take a glove off, and a storm is only what that gets to when there is enough of it. The people who work the stones are less easy, because a stone is supposed to be the last of what a creature was, and this creature is made of cold, and cold does not jump. What reached the bottom of it was the reaching. Past the thing in front of it, for the thing behind it.

It hunts without stopping, and there is very little up there to hunt. It moves hunched and unhurried and makes no sound on the snow, and what those claws open does not close quickly, because the cold gets into the wound and settles in. Talons drop out of it and grow back, so a patient tracker can follow one across a whole season by the sockets left in the drift behind it, ragged, always in sets. None of what it catches makes any difference. It has been starving the entire time and will go on starving, because there is nothing in there that could ever be full. When it goes down it goes all at once and stays down, and the heap darkens as it settles, and dark carries a long way up there. That is how the position gets reported at all, and the position is the trouble: a great many days uphill, on the far side of the massif from the eastern ground where this is supposed to happen, over country more of the dead have agreed on, for longer, than any other in the world. People used to call the high snow safe on exactly that reasoning, too well remembered to lose. The ones who still say it have not been up lately.

stone_golem.description: A cairn that got up. Moss on every weathered face, a flat head low in the shoulders, one fist that opens ground.
lore: Count the dead who ever cleared stones off a field before they could work it, and you have counted a good share of everybody. Every one of those fields had a heap at the edge of it — near enough the same heap in every country and every century: rounded brown stones, waist-high, added to a little each season. Seen daily by whoever worked the ground. Walked around, never walked on, put to no further use after the first stone went onto it. Enough of that, in enough fields, for long enough, and one of the heaps has a face in it.

There was never anyone in it, and the proof is public, and it is not a pleasant thing to watch. When one of these goes down the head goes first — it tips off the shoulders, lands, rolls a little — and for a moment there is a black socket where it was sitting. Everybody leans in the first time. The dark in it is about as deep as your hand and then it is stone: no cavity, no worn place shaped to fit anyone, nothing that was ever occupied. Then the body follows in a run of rubble, and what is on the ground is a heap again, moss and all, about the size it must have started at. It stays a heap for a good long while. It does not always stay one.

Among the fallen stones there is usually something harder than the rest. A split geode still leaking cold light. A six-sided point of white quartz. A teal crystal with a working edge on it. Now and then raw gold sitting in rubble-grade rock, which is the find people go up for. The ones who crack them for a living hold that a thing like this has to gather around something to begin with, and that it takes whatever in the ground is hardest and least arguable and grows outward from there. Gold is the one substance the dead of every century remember the same way. If you were assembling a body out of nothing but agreement, that is where you would start too. And past all of that, at the middle, there is one thing more: mossed plates shut around a small yellow-green star, warm to hold. Growth is not the soft half of anything. Watch a root take a wall apart and you know what green does to stone, given time; the star hands that over all at once, out of the edge of a blade, and then spends the rest of the fight closing you up while you are busy elsewhere.

Look at where the green is. The crown, the shoulder tops, the outsides of the arms, one flank — the faces that catch weather, and none of the faces that do not. Moss does not grow on a thing that moves. It grew there in the field, through season after season of holding one attitude, and it is the only part of the whole arrangement that was ever alive. Which is about right for what anybody keeps of a big old rock at the edge of a field. Not the rock. The rock was never in question. What stays with you is that it was green on one side, and that things were living on it.

stone_turtle.description: Hot stone in a tortoise's shape, orange banked in every seam. Still keeping a crossing that stopped being used.
lore: Of the ways over the gorge, at least one is no longer taken. The path up to it went somewhere else in a Turn, the walk round came out shorter than the walk up, and the crossing has carried nothing but weather since. There is a tortoise on it, made of hot stone, old past estimating. It does not hurry and it does not give chase, and a great deal goes past it with nothing happening at all. Some things do not. When one of those comes along, the seams in the shell come up bright all the way over the skull, and by then it is generally too late to have wanted the other route.

It was never posted there. The guards on the crossings people still use are the ordinary sad kind — a shape still doing a duty that outlived whoever gave it — and this one gets filed in with them at a glance and does not belong in the file. What put it on that ledge was the picture. For a long stretch of years, everybody who described a high crossing also described what waits on one, and the versions agreed better than the describers would have admitted: something old, something slow, something you do not argue with. Then the crossing emptied and the describing carried on without it, and all that attention had nothing left to attach to. It came up out of the ground into the gap and took the post. There is no duty in it and nothing owed to anyone. There is an expectation being met, in stone, by a thing with no idea it is meeting one.

Plates shed off it as the fire underneath them cools — black glass, mostly, and now and then one comes away whole in the shape of an egg. Nothing has ever hatched out of one. Nothing was going to: an old tortoise with a clutch under it is part of the picture people brought here, and this is that picture the whole way down, eggs included. There is one real egg and it is at the middle. Crack the shell and the rest of it slumps and runs and goes out, and what is sitting in the cooling puddle when it stops is charred black, split open by live orange, and too warm to be sensible about carrying. Set against a blade it does the one thing the whole shape was ever full of: what you strike goes on burning after you have stopped. The orange itself is the harder question. It runs through shell and skull alike, and it is the stone of the stretch of massif that is the wrong colour and warm to stand on, a very long way down and a long way off. How a piece of that ground came to be holding a crossing this high, and whether it walked here, has no answer anybody trusts.

tree_stump.description: Cut flat on top by an axe that was never swung. Two dark eyes, no mouth, and root-legs that lash for its moss.
lore: Reason backwards from a stump and you get a trunk, and there was never a trunk. What a great many people had instead was a wood — not one particular wood, the general one: the smell of it after rain, the bars of light coming down, the sound your own boots make in it. Enough of that settled in one place that there is a wood standing there now, and there was some left over when the wood was finished, and the leftover got up on roots. Its top is cut flat, and no axe has ever been swung in that wood. Open it and there is planed oak inside, the grain running true, dressed timber out of a tree that never grew. Nothing did that to it. The oak came in with everything else, because a forest does not get remembered on its own account: people remember a forest they had a use for, the clearing and the woodpile and the boards stacked under the eaves, and whatever comes up out of all that carries the whole of it, including the parts that only make sense if somebody had been working there.

Two eyes and nothing else on its face. No mouth, which unsettles people rather more than teeth would. It goes about on its roots at the pace of a thing with nowhere to be, carrying a small country on its back: a fat violet cap growing out of the moss on one shoulder, a paper hornet nest under the rim with one dark doorway low on the side and nothing at home in it most of the time, a knuckled little root that trots along at its foot and could as easily be a passenger as a relation. Crowd any of that and the roots come up and it lashes, harder than a thing its size has any business doing. Press it past holding and it does not fly apart. It sits down. It settles and shortens and goes on shortening, patiently, until what is left is a stump cut level with the ground in a wood that was never worked, and in the middle of that sits the hard piece: mossy green, warm in the hand, a red vein running out through it in branches the way roots run. Set against a blade it strikes harder than it ought to, and some of what it opens closes on your side instead. The people who work the stones file it with the blood-natured ones and are not entirely comfortable doing so, since the only thing that ever ran in the creature was sap.

What it is not doing is thinning. Nothing in it has gone missing, because nothing was ever in it: no name it fails to produce, no round it still walks for a keeper it can no longer picture. It cannot be got at that way at all. It holds for as long as the wood behind it holds, and that wood stands in the low country, where the ground is soft in both senses and changes most from one Turn to the next. What becomes of a thing like this when its wood goes elsewhere is a question that comes up late at a fire and is still open when the fire is out. The tellers hold that it could remember itself whole and go on, the same as anybody. The obvious objection is that there is nothing in it to do the remembering with; the tellers have heard that objection and are unmoved by it. Neither side has watched it happen. Meanwhile it hauls itself between the trees at its own pace, mushroom and empty nest and little root, entirely untroubled by the question — nothing in it was ever built for worrying, and somebody else has to do that part.

water_poring.description: Two big eyes in a wobble of pond water. Corner it and it bursts into spray, then gathers itself back up.
lore: This is the first of them most new stars meet, and the one that has to be explained twice. Nothing fell to make it. No creature drowned in that water and came back small and round; there was never anybody in there at all. A low wet place got remembered by a great many people and walked past by none of them for a long while, and the remembering pooled the way water pools, and one morning it had a face on it.

Fight one and it bursts. It is alarming exactly once. The whole thing comes apart into spray, sits a moment as a flat wet patch on the ground, and is a blob again before you have finished deciding how you feel about it. Nothing you do to it lands the way it looks like it lands, because there is nothing in it for anything to land on.

People who sort creatures for a living get one question into the usual list and stop. What has it lost, they ask — and the question has nowhere to go, because there was never anything in it to be losing. It holds together for exactly as long as the remembering it condensed out of stays pooled where it is, and when that goes elsewhere it comes apart. Whether that is an ending, and whose, gets argued at fires and settles nothing.

It is water gathered round stones and it leaves both. There is a smooth grey-blue river stone it carries about the way it carries everything, for no reason it could give; the frogs down there keep one too, which is either evidence of something or the least interesting coincidence in the valley. Under that is the hard piece — dull brown plates veined with copper, egg-sized, warm, and much heavier in the palm than the whole creature looked from ten paces. Worked into armour it makes a person very difficult to shift, and that is the one true thing about a puddle, kept. A puddle is not brave and it is not stubborn. It simply cannot be pushed off its own low place, and it is back in it whatever the weather does, and it will still be there when everything that used to walk past it has gone.

white_rabbit.description: Tame in a way nothing wild is: it comes closer than it should, bolts, and bites in earnest when it cannot run.
lore: The white is a poor idea in country that has things hunting in it, and the coat comes away with the cold still in it: a burr of fur, blue down in its shadows, that takes its time finishing the thaw in your palm. None of that is the strange part. The strange part is that it comes toward you.

Nothing wild does that. A rabbit is an animal that has decided in advance about every noise there is, and this one decides correctly about all of them, and then for a moment decides wrong. It drifts three or four steps in your direction with its ears up, the way an animal moves toward a person it is expecting something from, and then whatever is left inside catches up with it and it is forty feet away. Watch that happen twice and you know a thing about it that it does not know about itself. Somebody kept this one, and whoever it was got forgotten before the rabbit did.

The rest of what it does is a routine with the middle taken out. Twice a day it comes onto the same patch of open ground, faces the same way, and waits. Nothing arrives. After a while it goes and eats. People who have sat and watched it will tell you the hour is exact, and not one of them can tell you what the hour was for, and neither can it. Loyalty would need somebody in there to be loyal; what is keeping the appointment is the shape a loyalty leaves behind, still perfectly on time. It has also put by a store of hard brown kernels, which was never a rabbit's food. Half the small things in the low country are hoarding something they cannot eat.

It bolts from everything, which is why people underestimate it, and it will not turn while it still has somewhere to run. Take that away and it turns. The teeth are real and were always real, and there is no gentler lesson available in this country than the one a white rabbit hands somebody in their first season, which is that nearly everything here will hurt you eventually and almost none of it means to.

An animal that never fought anything in its existence is nonetheless the finest authority in the world on weight: how much roof will hold, how far a thing can drop and still run, what to do about the weight coming down. That turns out to be what the stone is — a plate of grey granite seamed with salmon pink, the exact pink of the inside of its ears, which people notice and then decide not to make anything of. Worked into armour it does for whoever wears it what the burrow did for the rabbit. Falls come off shorter. The blow meant to crush arrives merely heavy.

entries.name: The Falling
entries.summary: Nobody walks into Nangijala. You fall into it, once, and the whole sky sees you do it.
body: Nobody walks into Nangijala. You fall into it, once, and the whole sky sees you do it.

Look up on any clear night and wait. Sooner or later a line of light will open at one horizon and close at the other, and somewhere under it a person is sitting up in the grass with no idea where they are. That is all an arrival is. There is no gate, no ferryman, no one taking names. There is a streak of light that everybody sees, and then there is somebody new.

You arrive with what you were wearing and nothing else. Whatever you were carrying at the end stays at the end. Some people come down with a coat and a good pair of boots and consider themselves fortunate for a hundred years afterwards.

What you mostly do not arrive with is your name. This surprises people who have not seen it happen. The name is not taken; it simply does not always make the journey, and a new star will sit for an hour trying to produce it the way you try to produce a word you have known your whole life. Some get it back. Some never do, and go on quite happily as whatever the first person to reach them called them.

Which is why we go and meet them. It is the oldest courtesy in Nangijala and the only one that everybody still keeps: when you see a star come down, you walk to where it landed. You tell them what has happened. You tell them it is not going to hurt. And then, before it goes, you ask them for their name and one true thing about themselves, and you listen properly while they say it.
It costs nothing and it is the single most useful thing one person can do for another here, for reasons that took this world a very long time to work out.

Not every star has somebody in it. On some nights you will see one fall and go to the place and find nothing at all — no one in the grass, no track, nothing bent. Those are called wild stars. The tellers say they are people who arrived with too little left to arrive with. Nobody enjoys talking about it, and everybody goes and looks anyway, every time, in case this one is different.

There is a fire burning at the place where new stars come down. Somebody lit it a very long time ago so that the first thing anyone saw here would be a light with a person beside it. Whether that somebody is still around is a question this book will come back to.

entries.name: The Age of Coming
entries.summary: Why one afternoon's walk crosses an aqueduct, a windmill, a line of telegraph poles and a ring of standing stones.
body: Walk east from the meadow for an afternoon and you will pass under a broken aqueduct, through a field of standing stones, past a windmill nobody has turned in living memory, and along a line of poles strung with wire that goes from nowhere to nowhere. None of these things belong to the same world. All of them are here.
This is not a curiosity. It is the plainest evidence we have for how Nangijala is built, and the first thing a new star should be told once they have stopped shaking.

The dead arrive from everywhere and every when. They arrive remembering, and here, remembering is not a private event. A thing held firmly enough in enough minds simply is. Somebody came down out of the sky knowing exactly what an aqueduct was, and knew it so well and for so long that there is an aqueduct. Somebody else, falling a very long way from them in every sense, brought a windmill.
Neither of them was wrong. The world does not choose between them. It builds both, side by side, and lets the grass grow up through whichever one is being thought about less.

The oldest of us call the first stretch of the world's history the Age of Coming, and everything good to look at dates from it. It was an age with no maintenance and no scarcity, because nobody had yet noticed that anything needed maintaining. People fell, and the country got larger and stranger and more beautiful, and the building was tremendous.

You can still read what people brought. Somebody remembered a lighthouse hard enough that there is a lighthouse standing in the shallows, warning nothing, its lamp cold. Somebody brought a triumphal arch and set it in a field for a victory that happened in a country that is not here. Somebody brought a well, and a shrine of stacked stones, and a scarecrow, and a great oak with a house in it. There is a statue standing in the ice with a face nobody recognises, and everyone agrees it must have been important to whoever carried it here.

That is the second thing the ruins tell you, and it is less comfortable than the first. Everything built in the Age of Coming was built out of one person's certainty. When the certainty went, the building stayed — for a while.

The age ended without ceremony. Things began, here and there, to go soft. A wall that had stood since anyone could remember was suddenly not as tall as it had been, and then was a heap, and then was a green place where a heap used to be. Nobody understood it. There was a long stretch of the world's history during which the finest minds in Nangijala believed the answer had something to do with the sea.
It did not. What was happening was much simpler, and once somebody finally said it out loud, everything changed.

entries.name: The Age of Fires
entries.summary: The discovery that held the world together, and the argument that came with it.
body: The discovery, when it finally came, was so plain that it embarrassed everybody who had spent centuries on the sea theory.
The things people talk about stay.

That is the whole of it. A thing remembered by one person alone holds its shape for a while and then begins to go. A thing spoken about — told, aloud, to somebody who is actually listening — holds very much longer, and a thing told often enough by enough people does not go at all. The high crossings over the gorge have stood through everything because for a great many years there was never a week when somebody was not telling somebody else about the crossings over the gorge.
What followed is remembered as the Age of Fires, and it was the best of us.

The fires were lit — real ones, because you cannot get people to sit down and listen in the dark and the cold — and there was a rota. That word does not sound like the foundation of a civilisation, but that is exactly what it was. Somebody was responsible for each fire. Somebody walked a circuit between them. When a star came down, a keeper went to it, told the new arrival what had happened to them, and asked for their name and one true thing while they could still say it, and then carried that name to the next fire and said it there.
Whole districts of Nangijala were held up, stone by stone, by people who were good at talking in the evening. Some of them are still standing.
It is worth being honest about the flaw, because everybody here has an opinion about it and a new star will be asked their view within a month.

A told story grows. It is retold slightly warmer, slightly braver, slightly better shaped, every time, by people who mean nothing but well. Keep a man alive by telling him for forty years and at the end of it you have a man — solid, present, in no danger of going anywhere — who is not quite the man who fell. The fire-keepers know this. Most of them have decided it is a price worth paying, and a few of them have decided it very defensively.

So there came a second party, who said: write it down. Set it down exactly, once, and it is safe from all of you. And they were right, and they were thorough, and they made the Chronicle, which is the book you are reading now.

And then they found the thing that nobody has yet explained. A person recorded perfectly — every detail fixed, nothing drifting, the record sitting there entire and correct — goes Quiet anyway, on the usual schedule, with their own complete and beautiful account open on the shelf beside them.
The fire-keepers say the reason is obvious and that they have been saying it the whole time. It was never the accuracy. It was the listening.

The Chroniclers, who are not fools, have never accepted this, because it is not an explanation, it is a slogan. The argument is unresolved. It is the only argument in Nangijala that everybody has taken a side in, and you will be asked.

entries.name: The Quiet
entries.summary: You cannot die here. Something else can happen to you instead, and it is worse, and it is what most of the creatures in the world already are.
body: You cannot die in Nangijala. That door is behind you and it does not open twice. New stars find this reassuring for about a season.

It does not mean nothing can happen to you. You can be broken — knocked about past the point of holding a shape — and it is as unpleasant as it sounds and it is not an ending. What is left of you goes where the remembering is thickest, which in practice means the nearest fire somebody is tending, and puts itself back together beside it over a few hours. You keep what you were carrying. You lose a little of what you were thinking about. Nobody here treats a fight as final, and everybody here knows exactly how far it is to the nearest lit fire.

What can still happen to you is this. You can be forgotten — by everyone else, and then, in the end, by yourself — until there is nothing holding your shape but habit. It takes a long time and it does not hurt at any point, which is the part people find hard to hear.
It goes in four stages, and they have been called the same four things for as long as anybody has been counting.

You begin Bright. You know who you were and you can say it: your name, your work, the face of somebody you loved, the road home. Most people who fall are Bright for a very long time, particularly if somebody is telling them.

Then you Fade. The particulars go first, and they go so gently you cannot catch them at it. You know that you loved someone. You cannot produce the face. You know there was a road home and you could not now say which direction it ran. A faded person is entirely themselves, and entirely present, and simply has less and less to say about it.

Then there is Habit, and this is where it stops being sad and starts being frightening, because at some point the person is gone and the behaviour is still running. A thing that still walks its round. A thing that still guards its bridge, faithfully, for a keeper whose name went out of the world before it did. A thing that still comes home in the evening to a house that is not there any more and stands in the place where the door used to be.
This is what almost everything you will meet in the wild already is.

It is worth saying plainly, because new stars arrive with ideas about monsters. The creatures out there are not wicked. Very nearly none of them chose anything. Some are shapes that outlasted their occupants and kept doing the last thing they were doing. Others never had an occupant at all, and this world will be explaining those to you for some time. Either way they will come at you for reasons that stopped being reasons a long while back. Do not hate them. They are what happens.

And then, at the end, the Quiet. The shape lets go. There is no body and no grave, because there was no death; the thing simply stops being anywhere, and afterwards the place it was seems slightly wider than it should. People who have watched it happen say the worst part is how ordinary it looks.

The Quiet is what this world is afraid of. Not the creatures, not the cave, not the winter. Every fire, every rota, every argument between the tellers and the Chroniclers, every stranger who walks half a night to meet a falling star — all of it is the same species of answer to the same single question.
Which is: who is going to remember me, and for how long, and will they do it out loud.

entries.name: The Hard Pieces
entries.summary: What a soulstone is, why it is warm, and why an entire economy grew up around breaking open things that cannot fight back properly.
body: Everything that thins gets thinner all the way down and then stops. At the very bottom there is one thing left that will not go any further, and if you break the shape open it falls out into the grass. It is about the size of an egg. It is warm.

This is a soulstone, and of everything you can pick up in Nangijala it is the one thing guaranteed not to fade. There is an exception, and people who have been near the eastern mountain will tell you about it whether you ask or not.

It is not a soul. A soul is a whole person and no person ends up in a stone. What is in there is the last piece — one fact, one appetite, one habit of being, pressed down over centuries until it is very nearly a mineral. A thing that spent its existence burning leaves a stone that is still, in some stubborn way, about burning. A thing that endured cold leaves a stone that endures it.

Because a soulstone cannot be forgotten, it cannot decay, and in a world where everything else is quietly going soft that makes it the most valuable substance there is. Work one into a blade or set it into armour and it will lend you a little of what it remembers. It does not make you stronger. It makes you harder to argue with.

One kind of creature gives one kind of stone, and no two kinds give the same one. Nobody decided this. It is simply what it looks like when a particular way of forgetting reaches the bottom, and it means that a stone is a fair record of a kind of creature in a way that a drawing or a description never is.
The people who do this for a living have two words for the work, and you can tell a great deal about somebody from which one they use in front of you.

The polite word is releasing. It is not dishonest. A thing at the stage of Habit has nothing left in it, and the shape it is wearing is going to let go regardless; break it and the last hard piece is saved instead of lost with everything else. Put like that it is a mercy, and a good many people who do it have thought about it carefully and concluded exactly that.
The other word is cracking, and it is what the same people say to each other.

The distance between those two words is the entire moral range of the profession and there is no point pretending otherwise. Everybody carrying a bag of warm stones has made their peace with it in their own way, and the ones who talk about it least have usually thought about it most.

Then there is the rest of what comes off them. Teeth, hide, bone, quills, feathers, cracked stone, a knife somebody was still carrying. Junk, and worth almost nothing, and collected by absolutely everybody.

It is not the material that is wanted. It is that a pile of a creature's leavings is a story with the details still on it — this one had a jaw like that, this one carried a blade of that make — and details are precisely what goes first. Somebody, somewhere, is buying every scrap of it, and has been for a long time, and has never satisfactorily explained what for.

entries.name: The Gold Agreement
entries.summary: Nangijala did not choose a currency. It discovered the one substance nobody has ever managed to misremember.
body: Nangijala never decided on money. There was no mint, no decree, nobody with the authority to declare anything legal tender to anybody. What happened instead is that somebody eventually noticed a peculiar fact about gold, and the fact did the rest.
Gold is the only thing that everybody remembers the same.

Consider what that means in a country built the way this one is. Two people fall a thousand years and half a world apart. Ask them for a road and you will get two roads. Ask them for a house, a boat, a loaf, a king, and you will get two of each, and both will be real, and they will sit in the same field disagreeing with one another forever.
Ask them both for a gold coin and you get the same coin.

Weight, colour, the particular soft way it takes a mark from a thumbnail, the fact that it will not tarnish and will not go green and will not go anywhere at all — everybody who ever handled it came away with an identical impression, and they carried that identical impression down out of the sky. Gold is the one point in the whole of human memory where there is no argument to have.

So gold does not drift. It is the only common thing here that doesn't. Every other object in your possession is being held in shape by somebody's attention and will begin to go soft the moment that attention wanders, but a coin is a coin is a coin, and will still be exactly a coin when the house you are standing in has become a green place where a house used to be.
That is the whole reason it is money. Not scarcity — there is a great deal of it, and more falling all the time. It is money because it is the only thing you can put in a box and come back to.

There is a joke among the tellers that gold is the one honest thing in Nangijala because it is the only object nobody has ever managed to improve in the retelling. Like most jokes here it is repeated a little too often by people who are not laughing.

entries.name: The Long Morning
entries.summary: There is a further shore, and the way to it is open to anybody, and almost nobody goes.
body: Nangijala is not the last place. This is not in dispute, which is unusual for anything in this book.

Every so often somebody here stops being here. Not the Quiet — nothing like the Quiet. A person who is entirely Bright, entirely themselves, who has got all the way back to their own name and their own face and the road home and does not need one other living soul to hold any of it for them, will one evening simply not be in the room, and everybody who knew them will find that they remember them perfectly and feel no grief at all, which is the strangest part of the whole business.
And that night the northern sky lights up.

The tellers call it the Long Morning, and they call the lights the far edge of somebody else's dawn, seen from underneath. It is a beautiful thing to say and there is no evidence for it whatsoever. Nobody has come back. Not once, not ever, not a word.
The Chroniclers regard that silence as disqualifying and have said so at length. The fire-keepers regard it as the entire point, and have said so at greater length.

What is not in dispute is that the way is open, and that it is open to everybody, and that it appears to cost nothing at all. Remember yourself completely and you may go on. That is the requirement, and it is the only requirement, and it has never once been observed to fail.

So the question a new star always eventually asks — usually about a year in, usually at somebody's fire, usually with the face of a person who thinks they have spotted something everybody else has missed — is why on earth is anybody still here.
The answers are not complicated. Almost nobody's is.

There are people waiting for somebody who has not fallen yet, and who will not go on ahead of them, and who have been standing at the meeting-places for a very long time getting slowly stranger. There are people who did fall, and whose person fell too, and thinned, and is still out there as a shape doing something faithful and empty; and they will not leave a thing that still has their name in its mouth. There are people who did something in the life before this one and cannot make going on feel like anything but getting away with it.
And there are the keepers, who could go tomorrow, and who have the rota.

Ask anybody here why they are still here and they will tell you, if you have sat with them long enough. Everybody in Nangijala has an answer to that question. It is the answer that makes them a person rather than a shape.

entries.name: The Hole Under the Mountain
entries.summary: There is one mouth in the east massif, everybody knows where it is, and the ground around it forgets on a clock you can time with a candle.
body: Everything else in this book is the world working as it always has. This chapter is not that.

There is a cave under the eastern mountain. It has one mouth, it is not hidden, and every single person in Nangijala can tell you roughly where it is. There is no legend about finding it. The whole difficulty has always been the other direction.
Near it, things forget faster.

That is the plain observation, and it was made carefully, by people who did not want it to be true. Ground that had been held for centuries — good ground, in the rota, with a fire on it — went soft in a season. Then the season became a month. A keeper working the eastern circuit reported that she had lost the name of her own fire while walking toward the mouth and had it back within an hour of walking away, and she was not a woman anybody had ever known to lose anything.
Things that go in come out wrong, or come out wearing something else's face, or do not come out.

The creatures around it are not like the creatures anywhere else, and anybody who has been near both can tell the difference immediately. Out in the world a beast is a shape that outlasted its occupant — it is running on habit, it is empty, and there is something almost restful about how uninterested it is in you. The things near the mouth are not empty in that way. They were emptied. It happened to them, all at once, and something is still wearing the outside.

When you break one, a mask comes down out of it and lands in the dirt, and it is still smiling. This is the detail that started the entire investigation, because the mask does not thin. Nothing about it goes soft. It sits there afterwards being exactly a face, indefinitely, long after everything else about the creature has stopped being anywhere at all.
There is a great deal of argument about what is down there and none of it is worth writing down yet. Two things, though, are worth stating, because both are checkable and both are unsettling.

The first is that the hole is new. Not new the way a season is new — new the way a wound is. The Age of Fires had no hole under the eastern mountain. There are people still walking around, thinning quietly, who remember when the east road was simply a road, and if you buy them an evening they will tell you what the ground there used to feel like.

The second is that whatever is down there is not angry with anybody. Nothing about it is angry. It has never once been observed to do anything out of malice, or vengeance, or any of the ordinary reasons a thing does harm.
It is hungry. That is all it is. The tellers say that is worse, and the tellers are right.

entries.name: The Chronicle
entries.summary: A note on the book you are holding: who writes it, why they write it, and what an empty page in it actually means.
body: A word about this book, since you are already in it.

The Chronicle is the work of the Chroniclers, who hold that a thing written down exactly is a thing saved exactly, and who have been setting Nangijala down page by page for a long time now. Every creature described here was gone and looked at by somebody. Every account of the ages was assembled out of what people at fires could still be got to say. It is not a story anybody made up. It is a record, kept badly at the edges and very well in the middle, by people who took it seriously.
They are, it should be said, not universally loved for it. The tellers hold that a written thing stops growing, and they are not wrong. There is a stiffness to a page that there is not to an evening.

But consider what the alternative has cost. There are districts of this world that were held up for centuries by three people who were good at talking, and when those three thinned, the district went, and there is now nothing there but good grazing and a name nobody can source. The Chronicle exists because somebody looked at that and decided they would rather have a stiff and complete account of a place than a warm and vanished one.
So: read it, and treat what it says as true, because it was checked.

And when you find a page with nothing on it — a creature with no account, a place with no history, a name with no person attached — understand what you are looking at. It does not mean that nothing is known. It means no chronicler has got there yet. There are a great many more things in Nangijala than there are people willing to sit down and write about them, and the gap has been widening for some time.
If you know something that is not in here, the Chroniclers would like to hear it. That is not a formality. It is very nearly the entire method.

entries.name: The Human Dead
entries.summary: No claws, no scales, nothing in the blood. What humans brought to Nangijala instead was a habit of telling each other things, and it turned out to be the only thing that mattered.
body: Of everything that falls out of the sky into Nangijala, the human dead are neither the oldest nor the strongest nor the strangest, and they know it. A human arrives with no claws, no scales, nothing in the blood, and nothing to trade on but nerve and a quick pair of hands.
What they do have is a habit, and the habit turns out to be the most important fact about this world.

Humans talk. Not usefully, most of the time — they talk about the weather, and about people who are not present, and about what happened to them once in a place that no longer exists. They do it at the ends of days. They do it around fires, without being asked, as though something in them cannot sit in front of a light with another person and stay quiet.

In any other country that would be a pleasant nothing. Here it is maintenance. Every one of those idle evenings is a thing being held in shape, and the reason so much of Nangijala is still standing is that a species which cannot stop chattering fell into a world that is built out of being talked about. The fire-keepers did not invent the practice. They only noticed what everybody was already doing and wrote a rota for it.

It has made humans, on the whole, the ones who go and meet the stars. Not out of any particular virtue — they are as petty here as anywhere and the arguments in this world are almost all theirs — but because a human who sees a light come down over the next field is constitutionally incapable of not walking over to see who it was.

They are also the ones who fight, which follows from the same thing rather than from any talent for it. A human will go a long way out of their way for somebody they have sat with. Give them a reason and a blade and they will walk into the black rock after a thing that has nothing left in it, and come back with a warm stone in their pocket and a story about it, and tell the story that night, and hold up a corner of the world for another year without ever once thinking of it that way.

They fall young and they fall old and they fall in every state of readiness. Most arrive with nothing but what they stand in. Nearly all of them, given a season and somebody to listen, get their name back.
